G153: αἰσχύνω [ῡ]: — Ionic dialect imperfect αἰσχύνεσκε (κατ-) [ [4th c.AD(?): Quintus Smyrnaeus Epicus 14.531]]: future -ῠνῶ[ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hippolytus” 719]], Ionic dialect -υνέω[ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 9.53]]: aorist ᾔσχῡνα[ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 23.571, 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 1.4, etc.]]: perfect σχυγκα[ [2nd-3rd c.AD: Dio Cassius Historicus 58.16]]:—passive, future αἰσχῠνοῦμαι[ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 856, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Fragmenta” 200, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Timaeus” 49d, etc., rarely αἰσχυνθήσομαι (see. entry near the end)]]: aorist ᾐσχύνθην[ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus]] and Attic dialect, poetry infinitive αἰσχυνθῆμεν[ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “N.” 9.27:]]perfect ᾔσχυμμαι (see. below [ [5th c.BC: Bacchylides Lyricus I)]]:—make ugly, disfigure, πρόσωπον, κόμην, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 18.24, 27, compare 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 529]]; αἰ. τὸν ἵππον give the horse a bad form, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “de Equitandi ratione” 1.12.]] — __2 mostly in moral sense, dishonour, tarnish, μηδὲ γένος πατέρων αἰσχυνέμεν[ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 6.209, compare 23.571; τὴν Σπάρτην 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 9.53; ξενίαν τράπεζαν 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 401; τοὺς πρὸς αἵματος 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 1305; τοὺς πατέρας 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Menexenus” 246d.]] — __2.b especially dishonour a woman, [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Electra” 44, compare 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus “Marcellus” 19, etc.; εὐνήν 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 1626]]; εἰς τὸ σῶμα αἰ. [ [4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Politica” 1311b7; _absolutely_, “Foed. Delph.Pell.” 2 A 12.]] — __3 disdain, ἐπιχώρια[ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 3.22.]] — __B passive, to be dishonoured, νέκυς σχυμμένος, of Patroclus, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 18.180.]] — __B.II to be ashamed, feel shame, absolutely, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 7.305, 18.12, 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.10, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hippolytus” 1291.]] — __B.II.2 more commonly, to be ashamed at a thing, with accusative of things, αἰσχυνόμενοι φάτιν ἀνδρῶν[ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 21.323; τὴν δυσγένειαν τὴν ἐμὴν αἰ. 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 1079: with _dative_ _of things_, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Nubes” 992, 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 3.9, 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 4.42, etc.; αἰ. ἐπί τινι 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 2.2.8; ἔν τινι 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 2.43; ὑπέρ τινος 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 14.39; περί τινος 33.6. etc.]] — __B.II.2.b with participle, to be ashamed at doing a thing (which one does), [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 642 (variant), 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 540, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Fragmenta” 200, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Grg.” 494e, etc.]] — __B.II.2.c with infinitive, to be ashamed to do a thing (and therefore not to do it), [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.82, 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 856, “Ch.” 917, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 414e, “Phdr.” 257d, etc.]]; though this condition must not be pressed absolutely,[ [compare “Ap.” 22b.]] — __B.II.2.d followed by relative clause, αἰσχύνεσθαι εἰ.. to be ashamed that.., [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Electra” 254, 5th-6th c.BC: Andocides Orator 4.42; ἐάν.. 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Oeconomicus” 21.4; μὴ.. 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 183e, cf. Machoap. 2nd c.AD: Athenaeus Epigrammaticus 13.579f; ὅτι.. 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 2.23.]] — __B.II.3 with accusative person, to feel shame before one, [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Ion” 934, 1074, 5th c.BC: Pherecrates Comicus 23.6, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Symposium” 216b]]; τοὺς γέροντας (at Sparta) [ [4th c.BC: Aeschines Orator 1.180]]; ὅστις γὰρ αὐτὸς αὑτὸν οὐκ αἰσχύνεται, πῶστόν γε μηδὲν εἰδότ᾽ αἰσχυνθήσετα; [ [4th-3rd c.BC: Philemo Comicus 229, compare 2nd c.AD: Galenus Medicus 5.26]]: with accusative et infinitive, [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Helena” 415; ᾑσχύνθημεν θεοὺς.. προδοῦναι αὐτόν 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 2.3.22; αἰσχύνομαι ὑμᾶς λέγειν 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 40.48; αἰ. πρός τινα 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Rhetorica” 1383b12.]]
G154: αἰτ-έω — (Aeolic dialect αἴτημι [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “Fragmenta.” 155, 3rd c.BC: Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus 28.5)]], Ionic dialect imperfect αἴτεον[ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus:]]future αἰτήσω: aorist ᾔτησα: perfect ᾔτηκα[ [NT.1John.5.15]]: pluperfect ᾐτήκει[ [2nd c.AD: Arrianus Historicus “Anabasis” 6.15.5:]]perfect passive ᾔτημαι, etc.:—ask, beg, absolutely, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 18.49, 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Supplices” 341.]] — __2 mostly with accusative of things, ask for, demand, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.358, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 17.365, etc.]]; ὁδὸν αἰ. ask leave to depart, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 10.17]]; αἰ. τινί τι to ask something for one,[ [20.74, 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 5.17]]: with accusative person et of things, ask a person for a thing, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 22.295, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 2.387, 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 3.1, etc.]]; δίκας αἰ. τινὰ φόνου to demand satisfaction from one for.., [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 8.114; αἰ. τι πρός τινος 6th c.BC: Theognis Elegiacus 556; παρά τινος 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.3.16; τὰ αἰτήματα ἃ τήκαμεν παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ NT.1John.5.15.]] — __3 with accusative person et infinitive, ask one to do, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 3.173, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Coloneus” 1334, “Ant.” 65, etc.; αἰ. παρά τινος δοῦναι 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Eryxias” 398e.]] — __4 with accusative only, beg of, [ [3rd c.AD(?): Diogenes Laertius 6.49.]] — __5 in Logic, postulate, assume, [ [4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Analytica Priora” 41b9 (_passive_), “Top.” 163a6, etc.]] — __II middle, ask for one's own use, claim, Λύσανδρον ἄρχοντα[ [5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 12.59]]; frequently almost = the active, and with the same construct., first in [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.90]] (παρ-),[ [9.34, 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 822, etc.; αἰτεῖσθαί τινα ὅπως.. Antiphol. 12 codices]]; πάλαισμα μἠποτε λῦσαι θεὸν αἰτοῦμαι[ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 880]]; frequently absolutely in participle, αἰτουμένῳ μοι δός[ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Choephori” 480, compare 2, “Th.” 260, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 63; αἰτουμένη που τεύξεται [prev. author] “Ant.” 778; αἰτησάμενος ἐχρήσατο 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 19.27; οὐ πῦρ γὰρ αἰτῶν, οὐδὲ λοπάδ᾽ αἰτούμενος 4th-3rd c.BC: Menander Comicus 476]]; αἰτεῖσθαι ὑπέρ τινος to beg for one, [ [5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 14.22.]] — __III passive, of persons, have a thing begged of one, αἰτηθέντες χρήματα[ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 8.111, compare 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 2.97, etc.; αἰτεύμενος 3rd c.BC: Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus 14.63]]: with infinitive, to be asked to do a thing, [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “I.” 8(7).5.]] — __III.2 of things, to be asked, τὸ αἰτεόμενον[ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 8.112]]; ἵπποι ᾐτημένοι borrowed horses, [ [5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 24.12.]]
G155: αἴτ-ημα, ατος, τό, — request, demand, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 566b, LXX.1Ki.1.17, NT.Luke.23.24, “PFlor.” 296.16 (6th c.AD).]] — __II in Logic and in Mathematics texts, postulate, assumption, [ [4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Analytica Posteriora” 76b23, 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus “Demetrius” 3, 2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Herm.” 74.]]
G156: αἰτί-α, ἡ, — responsibility, mostly in bad sense, guilt, blame, or the imputation thereof, i.e. accusation, first in [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “O.” 1.35 and 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus, see below (8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus uses αἴτιος):]] —Phrases: αἰτίαν ἔχειν bear responsibility for, τινός[ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Eumenides” 579, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 1312]]; but usually to be accused, τινός of a crime, φόνου[ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 5.70]]: with infinitive, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Vespae” 506]]; followed by ὡς.., [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Apologia” 38c]]; by ὡς with participle, [ [[prev. author] “Phdr.” 249d]]; ὑπό τινος by some one, [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Eumenides” 99, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 565b: reversely, αἰτία ἔχει τινά 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 5.70, 71; αἰ. φεύγειν τινός 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 1404]]; ἐν αἰτίᾳ εἶναι or γίγνεσθαι, [ [5th c.BC: Hippocrates Medicus “περὶ ἄρθρων ἐμβολῆς” 67, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 2.8.6]]; αἰτίαν ὑπέχειν lie under a charge, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Apologia” 33b, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 6.3.16; ὑπομεῖναι 4th c.BC: Aeschines Orator 3.139; φέρεσθαι 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 2.60]]; λαβεῖν ἀπό τινος[ [[prev. work] 18; αἰτίαις ἐνέχεσθαι 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Crito” 52a; αἰτίαις περιπίπτειν 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 7.1; εἰς αἰτίαν ἐμπίπτειν 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 150a; αἰτίας τυγχάνειν 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator “Epistulae” 2.2; ἐκτὸς αἰτίας κυρεῖν 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 332]]; ἐν αἰτίῃ ἔχειν hold one guilty, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 5.106; δι᾽ αἰτίας ἔχειν 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 2.60, etc.; ἐν αἰτίᾳ βάλλειν 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 656]]; τὴν αἰτίαν ἐπιφέρειν τινί impute the fault to one, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.26; αἰτίαν νέμειν τινί 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 28; ἐπάγειν 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 18.283; προσβάλλειν τινί 5th c.BC: Antipho Orator 3.2.4]]; ἀνατιθέναι, προστιθέναι, [ [5th c.BC: Hippocrates Medicus “περὶ ἀρχαίης ἰητρικῇς” 21, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Pax” 640, etc.]]; ἀπολύειν τινὰ τῆς αἰτίης to acquit of guilt, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 9.88, etc.]] — __2 in forensic oratory, invective without proof (opposed to ἔλεγχος), [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 22.23, compare 18.15.]] — __3 in good sense, εἰ.. εὖ πράξαιμεν, αἰτία θεοῦ the credit is his, [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Septem contra Thebas” 4]]; δι᾽ ὅντινα αἰτίαν ἔχουσιν Ἀθηναῖοι βελτίους γεγονέναι are reputed to have become better, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 503b, cf. Alcaeus1.119a, 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Metaphysica” 984b19]]; ὧν.. πέρι αἰτίαν ἔχεις διαφέρειν in which you are reputed to excel, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 169a]]; οἳ.. ἔχουσι ταύτην τὴν αἰ. who have this reputation, [ [[prev. author] “R.” 435e, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Andocides Orator 2.12; αἰτίαν λαμβάνειν 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Leges” 624a.]] — __4 expostulation, μὴ ἐπ᾽ ἔχθρᾳ τὸ πλέον ἢ αἰτίᾳ[ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.69.]] — __II cause, δι᾽ ἣν αἰτίην ἐπολέμησαν[ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus “Prooem.”, compare 3rd c.AD: Democritus Epigrammaticus 83, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Timaeus” 68e, “Phd.” 97a]] {αἰτιάζομαι}, etc.; on the four causes of [ [4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus see “Ph.” 194b16, “Metaphorical” 983a26:—αἰ. τοῦ γενέσθαι or γεγονέναι 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 97a; τοῦ μεγίστου ἀγαθοῦ τῇ πόλει αἰτία ἡ κοινωνία [prev. author] “R.” 464b:]] — _dative_ αἰτίᾳ for the sake of, κοινοῦ τινος ἀγαθοῦ[ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 4.87, compare 1st c.BC: Dionysius Halicarnassensis 8.29:—αἴτιον compare (αἴτιος 11.2) is used like{αἰτία}]] in the sense of cause, not in that of accusation. — __III occasion, motive, αἰτίαν ῥοαῖσι Μοισᾶν ἐνέβαλε gave them a the me for song, [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “N.” 7.11; αἰτίαν παρέχειν 2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Tyr.” 13.]] — __IV head, category under which a thing comes, [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 23.75.]] — __V case in dispute, ἡ αἰ. τοῦ ἀνθρώπου μετὰ τῆς γυναικός[ [NT.Matt.10.10.]]

G302: ἄν, [ᾰ], — Epic dialect, Lyric poetry, Ionic dialect, [ [4th c.AD(?): Arcadius Grammaticus]], Attic dialect; also κεν) Epic dialect, Aeolic dialect, Thess., κᾱ Doric dialect, Boeotian dialect, El.; the two combined in Epic dialect (below [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 11.2) and 4th c.AD(?): Arcadius Grammaticus]], εἰκ ἄν[ [“IG” 5(2).6.2, 15 (4th c.BC)]]:—modal Particle used with Verbs to indicate that the action is limited by circumstances or defined by conditions. In [ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus]] κε is four times as common as ἄν, in Lyric poetry about equally common. No clear distinction can be traced, but κε as an enclitic is somewhat less emphatic; ἄν is preferred by [ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus]] in negative clauses, κε (ν) with the relative. — __A In Simple Sentences, and in the Apodosis of Compound Sentences; here ἄν belongs to the Verb, and denotes that the assertion made by the Verb is dependent on a condition, expressed or implied: thus ἦλθεν he came, ἦλθεν ἄν he would have come (under conditions, which may or may not be defined), and so he might have come; ἔλθοι may he come, ἔλθοι ἄν he would come (under certain conditions), and so he might come. — __A.I WITH INDICATIVE: — __A.I.1 with historical tenses, generally imperfect and aorist, less frequently pluperfect, never perfect, see below, — __A.I.1.a most frequently in apodosis of conditional sentences, with protasis implying nonfulfilment of a past or present condition, and apodosis expressing what would be or would have been the case if the condition were or had been fulfilled. The imperfect with ἄν refers to continued action, in [ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus]] always in past time, except perhaps καί κε θάμ᾽ ἐνθάδ᾽ ἐόντες ἐμισγόμεθ᾽[ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 4. 178]]; later also in present time, first in [ [6th c.BC: Theognis Elegiacus 905]]; πολὺ ἂν θαυμαστότερον ἦν, εἰ ἐτιμῶντο it would be far more strange if they were honoured, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 489a]]; οὐκ ἂν νήσων ἐκράτει, εἰ μή τι καὶ ναυτικὸν εἶχεν he would not have been master of islands if he had not had also some naval power, [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.9]]. The aorist strictly refers only to past time, [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “N.” 11.24, etc.]]; εἰ τότε ταύτην ἔσχε τὴν γνώμην, οὐδὲν ἂν ὧν νυνὶ πεποίηκεν ἔπραξεν if he had then come to this opinion, he would have accomplished nothing of what he has now done, [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 4.5, +others]], but is used idiomatically with Verbs of saying, answering, etc., as we say I should have said, εἰ μὴ πατὴρ ἦσθ᾽, εἶπον ἄν σ᾽ οὐκ εὖ φρονεῖν[ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 755, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Symposium” 199d, “Euthphr.” 12d, etc.: the]]pluperfect refers to completed actions, as ὃ εἰ ἀπεκρίνω, ἱκανῶς ἂν ἤδη παρὰ σοῦ τὴν ὁσιότητα ἐμεμαθήκη I should have already learnt..,[ [[prev. work] 14c; εἰ ὁ ἀνὴρ ἀπέθανεν, δικαίως ἂν ἐτεθνήκει 5th c.BC: Antipho Orator 4.2.3.]] — __A.I.1.b the protasis is frequently understood: ὑπό κεν ταλασίφρονά περ δέος εἷλεν fear would have seized even the stout-hearted (had he heard the sound), [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 4.421]]; τὸ γὰρ ἔρυμα τῷ στρατοπέδῳ οὐκ ἂν ἐτειχίσαντο they would not have built the wall (if they had not won a battle), [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.11]]; πολλοῦ γὰρ ἂν ἦν ἄξια for (if that were so) they would be worth much, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 374d]]; οὐ γὰρ ἦν ὅ τι ἂν ἐποιεῖτε for there was nothing which you could have done, i. e. would have done (if you had tried), [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 18.43.]] — __A.I.1.c with no definite protasis understood, to express what would have been likely to happen, or might have happened in past time: ἢ γάρ μιν ζωόν γε κιχήσεαι, ἤ κεν Ὀρέστης κτεῖνεν ὑποφθάμενος for either you will find him alive, or else Orestes may already have killed him before you, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 4.546]]; ὃ θεασάμενος πᾶς ἄν τις ἀνὴρ ἠράσθη δάϊος εἶναι every man who saw this (the 'Seven against Thebes') would have longed to be a warrior, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Ranae” 1022]]; especially with τάχα, which see, ἀλλ᾽ ἦλθε μὲν δὴ τοῦτο τοὔνειδος τάχ᾽ ἂν ὀργῇ βιασθὲν μᾶλλον ἢ γνώμῃ φρενῶν, i. e. it might perhaps have come, [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 523]]; τάχα ἂν δὲ καὶ ἄλλως πως ἐσπλεύσαντες (i.e. διέβησαν) and they might also perhaps have crossed by sea (to Sicily) in some other way, [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 6.2, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedrus” 265b.]] — __A.I.1.d ἄν is frequently omitted in apodosi with Verbs expressing obligation, propriety, or possibility, as ἔδει, ἐχρῆν, εἰκὸς ἦν, etc., and sometimes for rhetorical effect, εἰ μὴ.. ᾖσμεν, φόβον παρέσχεν it had caused (for it would have caused) fear, [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hecuba” 1113. This use becomes more common in later Gk.]] — __A.I.2 with future indicative: — __A.I.2.a frequently in Epic dialect, usually with κεν, rarely ἄν, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 9.167, 22.66, indicating a limitation or condition, ὁ δέ κεν κεχολώσεται ὅν κεν ἵκωμαι]] and he will likely be angry to whom-soever I shall come, [ [[prev. work] 1.139]]; καί κέ τις ὧδ᾽ ἐρέει and in that case men will say,[ [4.176; ἐγὼ δέ κέ τοι καταλέξω 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 3.80]]; so in Lyric poetry, μαθὼν δέ τις ἂν ἐρεῖ[ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “N.” 7.68, compare “I.” 6(5).59.]] — __A.I.2.b rarely in codices of Attic dialect Prose writers, σαφὲς ἂν καταστήσετε[ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.140; οὐχ ἥκει, οὐδ᾽ ἂν ἥξει δεῦρο 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 615d, compare “Ap.” 29c, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 2.5.13; uncertain in 5th c.BC: Hippocrates Medicus “γυναικεῖα” 2.174: in later Prose, 2nd-3rd c.AD: Philostratus Sophista “V A” 2.21, S 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “M.” 9.225: also in Poetry, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Electra” 484, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Aves” 1313; οὐκ ἂν προδώσω 3rd c.BC: Herodas Mimographus 6.36 (correlated -δοίην):— for ἄν with]]future infinitive and participle see below — __A.II WITH SUBJUNCTIVE, only in Epic dialect, the meaning being the same as with the future indicative [ [(1.2a), frequently with _1st pers._, as εἰ δέ κε μὴ δώῃσιν, ἐγὼ δέ κεν αὐτὸς ἕλωμαι in that case]]I will take her myself, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.324]]; πείθευ, ἐγὼ δέ κέ τοι εἰδέω χάριν obey and if so I will be grateful, [ [14.235 (the _subjunctive_ is always introduced by δέ in this usage)]]; also with other persons, giving emphasis to the future, οὐκ ἄν τοι χραίσμῃ κίθαρις[ [3.54, +others]] — __A.III WITH OPTATIVE (never future, rarely perfect πῶς ἂν λελήθοι [με]; [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Symposium” 3.6):]] — __A.III.a in apodosis of conditional sentences, after protasis in optative with εἰ or some other conditional or relative word, expressing a future condition: ἀλλ᾽ εἴ μοί τι πίθοιο, τό κεν πολὺ κέρδιον εἴη[ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 7.28; οὐ πολλὴ ἂν ἀλογία εἴη, εἰ φοβοῖτο τὸν θάνατο; 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 68b:—in 8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus]] present and aorist optative with κε or ἄν are sometimes used like imperfect and aorist indicative with ἄν in Attic, with either regular indicative or another optative in the protasis: καί νύ κεν ἔνθ᾽ ἀπόλοιτο.. εἰ μὴ.. νόησε κτλ., i. e. he would have perished, had she not perceived, etc., [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.311, compare 5.388, 17.70]]; εἰ νῦν ἐπὶ ἄλλῳ ἀεθλεύοιμεν, ἦ τ᾽ ἂν ἐγὼ.. κλισίηνδε φεροίμην if we were now contending in another's honour, I should now carry.., [ [[prev. work] 23.274: so rarely in Trag., οὐδ᾽ ἂν σὺ φαίης, εἴ σε μὴ κνίζοι λέχος (for εἰ μὴ ἔκνιζε) 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Medea” 568.]] — __A.III.b with protasis in present or future, the optative with ἄν in apodosi takes a simply future sense: φρούριον δ᾽ εἰ ποιήσονται, τῆς μὲν γῆς βλάπτοιεν ἄν τι μέρος they might perhaps damage, [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.142, compare 2.60, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Apologia” 25b, “R.” 333e; ἢν οὖν μάθῃς.. οὐκ ἂν ἀποδοίην 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Nubes” 116, compare 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 1.26, +others]] — __A.III.c with protasis understood: φεύγωμεν· ἔτι γάρ κεν ἀλύξαιμεν κακὸν ἦμαρ[ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 10.269]]; οὔτε ἐσθίουσι πλείω ἢ δύνανται φέρειν· διαρραγεῖεν γὰρ ἄν for (if they should do so) they would burst, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 8.2.21]]; τὸν δ᾽ οὔ κε δύ᾽ ἀνέρε.. ἀπ᾽ οὔδεος ὀχλίσσειαν two men could not heave the stone from the ground, i. e. would not, if they should try, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 12.447; οὐδ᾽ ἂν δικαίως ἐς κακὸν πέσοιμί τι 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 240, compare 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 2.8: in 8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus]] sometimes with reference to past time, Τυδεΐδην οὐκ ἂν γνοίης ποτέροισι μετείη[ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.85.]] — __A.III.d with no definite protasis implied, in potential sense: ἡδέως δ᾽ ἂν ἐροίμην Λεπτίνην but I would gladly ask Leptines, [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 20.129]]; βουλοίμην ἄν I should like, Latin velim (but ἐβουλόμην ἄν I should wish, if it were of any avail, vellem); ποῖ οὖν τραποίμεθ᾽ ἄ; which way then can we turn? [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Euthydemus” 290a]]; οὐκ ἂν μεθείμην τοῦ θρόνου I will not give up the throne, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Ranae” 830]]; idiomatically, referring to the past, αὗται δὲ οὐκ ἂν πολλαὶ εἶεν but these would not (on investigation) prove to be many, [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.9]]; also in Trag., θᾶσσον ἢ λέγοι τις[ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hippolytus” 1186; τεὰν δύνασιν τίς.. κατάσχο; 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 605.]] — __A.III.h ἄν with future optative is probably always corrupt (compare [ [1.2b), as τὸν αὐτὸν ἂν ἐπαινέσοι (ἐπαινέσαι Bekk.) 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Leges” 719e]]; [ [5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 1.22.]] — __A.IV WITH infinitive and participle (sometimes adjective equivalent to participle, τῶν δυνατῶν ἂν κρῖναι[ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 577b) representing _indicative_ or _optative_:]] — __A.IV.1 present infinitive or participle: — __A.IV.1.a representing imperfect indicative, οἴεσθε τὸν πατέρα.. οὐκ ἂν φυλάττει; do you think he would not have kept them safe? G350: ἀνακρίνω, — examine closely, interrogate, especially judicially, Παυσανίαν [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.95, compare 5th c.BC: Antipho Orator 2.1.9, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Symposium” 201e; ἀ. τινὰ πόθεν ζῇ 4th-3rd c.BC: Diphilus Comicus 32.3]]; sound a person, [ [LXX.1Ki.20.12.]] — __2 inquire into, ἀ. τοὺς ἐργασαμένους[ [5th c.BC: Antipho Orator 2.3.2]]; τὴν [αἰτίαν] [ [1st c.BC: Philodemus Philosophus “περὶ ποιημάτων” 994 “fragment” 21, compare “Lib.” p.21 O.:]] —middle, ἀ. ποινὰ τίς ἔσται what remedy there shall be, [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 4.63.]] — __II examine magistrates so as to prove their qualification, [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 57.66 and 70.]] — __II.2 of the magistrates, examine persons concerned in a suit, so as to prepare the matter for trial, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Andocides Orator 1.101, 4th c.BC: Isaeus Orator 5.32]]; ὁ ἄρχων ἀνέκρινε πᾶσιν ὑμῖν καὶ ἀνακρίνας εἰσήγαγεν εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 48.31, compare 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Ἀθηναίων Πολιτεία” 56.6]]:—passive, ἀνεκρίθησαν αἱ ἀμφισβητήσεις[ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 48.23:]] —middle, οὐκ ἀνεκρίνατο ταύτην [τὴν γραφήν] he did not have it examined, of the prosecutor, [ [[prev. author] 21.103, compare 53.17.]] — __II.3 generally, examine, μάρτυρας[ [“SIG” 953.46 (from Calymna)]]; τινά 1[ [“Cor.” 9.3]]:—middle, [ [“Michel” 409.9 (from Cos).]] — __II.4 select, [ [3rd c.AD: Pseudo-Callisthenes Historicus 3.26.]] — __III in middle, absolutely, ἀνακρίνεσθαι πρὸς ἑωυτούς dispute, wrangle one with another, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 9.56.]]
G351: ἀνάκρισις, — poetry ἄγκρ-, εως, ἡ, (ἀνακρίνω[ [11.1)]] examination of the qualifications of magistrates, [ [2nd c.AD(?): Pollianus Epigrammaticus 8.85.]] — __II (ἀνακρίνω[ [11.2)]] previous examination of parties concerned in a suit, preparation of the matter for trial, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Symposium” 5.2, etc., compare “PSI” 4.392 (3rd c.BC), “OGI” 374 (_plural_), NT.Act.25.26]]; of the magistrate, ἀνάκρισιν διδόναι, παραδιδόναι, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Charmides” 176c, “Lg.” 855e]]; of the parties, εἰς ἀνάκρισιν ἥκειν[ [4th c.BC: Isaeus Orator 6.13, etc.]]; μηδ᾽ εἰς ἄγκρισιν ἐλθεῖν, i. e. should not even begin proceedings (where however the [ [Scholia explains ἐς ἄγκρισιν by ἐς μάχην,compare ἀνακρίνω 111), 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Eumenides” 364]]; οὐδ᾽ ἀ. μοι δώσεις you will not allow me the first forms of law, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Chrm.” [prev. cited]]] — __III generally, inquiry, examination, [ [[prev. author] “Phdr.” 277e.]] — __IV preliminary examination of a slave before sale, [ [“POxy.” 1463.12, etc.]] — __V examination, testing of magical ingredients, etc., [ [“PMag.Par.” 1.1992, 2007.]] — __VI quarrel, dispute, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 8.69]]; disputation, [ [1st c.BC: Philodemus Philosophus “Academicorum Index” p.72 M.]]

G687: ἆρᾰ, — interrogative Particle, implying anxiety or impatience, = Epic dialect and Lyric poetry ἦ ῥα: — __1 alone, it simply marks the question, the nature of which is determined by the context: e.g. in [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 35.44]] a negative answer is implied in the question ἆρ᾽ ἂν οἴεσθε..; but an affirmative in [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 4.6.4]] ἆ. βέβληκα δὶς ἐφεξῆ; compare ἆρ᾽ εὐτυχεῖς.. ἢ δυστυχεῖ; [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Phoenissae” 424.—To make it plainly _negative_, we have ἆ. μή..; 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Septem contra Thebas” 208, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 64c]]; and to make it plainly affirmative, ἆρ᾽ ο; ἆρ᾽ οὐχ; [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Coloneus” 791, “OT” 540]]; ἆρ᾽ οὐχ οὕτω; [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Philebus” 11d.]] — __2 ἆ. οὖ; is used to draw an affirmative inference, [ [[prev. author] “Grg.” 477a, “La.” 190b]]; also when a negative answer is expected, [ [[prev. author] “Chrm.” 159b]]; with a negative, ἆρ᾽ οὖν οὐ..; [ [[prev. author] “Phdr.” 263a, etc.]] — __3 in ἆρά γε, each Particle retains its force, γε serving to make the question more definite, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Plutus” 546, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 1.5.4, etc.]] — __4 less frequently with τίς interrogative, τίνος ποτ᾽ ἆρ᾽ ἔπραξε χειρί[ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 905]]; τίδ᾽ ἆρ᾽ ἐγὼ σ; [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Iphigenia Aulidensis” 1228; τίς ἆρ᾽ ὁ φεύγω; 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Vespae” 893]]; with ἤν, [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Rhesus” 118.]] — __5 in indirect questions, σκεψώμεθα τοῦτο ἆ... [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 70e, compare “R.” 526c, +others, 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Physica” 204b3, etc.]] — __II in Poets sometimes like{ἄρα}, [ [7th c.BC: Archilochus Lyricus 86, 89, 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 4.78, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Vespae” 3; τοιοῖσδε χρησμοῖς ἆ. χρὴ πεποιθένα; 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Choephori” 297, compare 435; τῷ δὲ ξιφήρης ἆρ᾽ ὑφειστήκει λόχος 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Andromache” 1114: in exclamations, βραδεῖαν ἡμᾶς ἆρ᾽ ὁ τήνδε τὴν ὁδὸν πέμπων ἔπεμψεν 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 738; ὀδυνηρὸς ἆρ᾽ ὁ πλοῦτος 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Phoenissae” 566, compare “El.” 1229, “Hipp.” 1086; ἦ δεινὸν ἆρ᾽ ἦν [prev. author] “fragment” 931; ἔμελλόν σ᾽ ἆ. κινήσειν 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Nubes” 1301, compare “Ach.” 347.]] — __B In Prose, ἆ. almost always stands first in the sentence, but[ [compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 467e]]; καὶ ὑπὲρ τούτων ἆ... G896: Βάαλ (Rec. βαάλ), ὁ, ἡ, indecl. (Heb. בַּעַל, lord), — Baal: Rom.11:4 (LXX). The fem. art. here agrees with the usage of LXX, where, following a similar Hebrew practice (בֹּשֶׁת for בַּעַל), αἰσχύνη appears to have been substituted in reading for the written Βάαλ (cf. 3Ki.18:19), and to account for the frequently use of the fem. art. bef. Β. The usage, however, is not general, and in the passage cited in Ro (3Ki.19:18), LXX reads τῷ Β. † — (From Abbott-Smith. LSJ has no entry)

G1063: γάρ — (γε, ἄρα), causal conjunction, used alone or with other Particles. — __I introducing the reason or cause of what precedes, for, τῷ γὰρ ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη· κήδετο γ. Δαναῶν [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.56, etc.]]; but frequently in explanation of that which is implied in the preceding clause, πολλάων πολίων κατέλυσε κάρηνα.. τοῦ γὰρ κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον [ [2.118, etc.: hence,]] — __I.b in simple explanations, especially after a Pronoun or demonstrative adjective, ἀλλὰ τόδ᾽ αἰνὸν ἄχος κραδίην καὶ θυμὸν ἱκάνει· Ἕκτωρ γ. ποτε φήσει [ [8.148, compare 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 2.163]]; ὃ δὲ δεινότατον.. ὁ Ζεὺς γ... [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Aves” 514; ὃ δὲ πάντων ἀδικώτατον ἔδοξε· τῶν γὰρ προγε γραμμένων ἠτίμωσε καὶ υἱούς 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus “Sulla” 31]]; frequently in introducing proofs or examples, μαρτύριον δέ· Δήλου γ. καθαιρομένης.. [ [[prev. author] 2.39, compare 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 20.10, etc.]]; in full, τεκμήριον δὲ τούτου τόδε· αἱ μὲν γ... [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 2.58]]; παράδειγμα τόδε τοῦ λόγου· ἐκ γ... [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.2; δηλοῖ δέ μοι τόδε· πρὸ γ... [prev. work] 3.]] — __I.c to introduce a detailed description or narration already alluded to, ὅμως δὲ λεκτέα ἃ γιγνώσκω· ἔχει γ. [ἡ χώρα] πεδία κάλλιστα.. [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 5.6.6, etc.]] — __I.d in answers to questions or statements challenging assent or denial, yes,.., no,.. , οὔκουν.. ἀνάγκη ἐστ;—ἀνάγκη γ. οὖν, ἔφη, ay doubtless it is necessary, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 2.1.7, compare § 4 and 13; indicating assent, ἔχει γ. 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedrus” 268a]]; ἱκανὸς γ., ἔφη, συμβαίνει γ., ἔφη, [ [[prev. author] “R.” 502b, 502c,compare “Ap.” 41a, etc.]]; οὔκουν δὴ τό γ᾽ εἰκός.—οὐ γ.: [ [[prev. author] “Phdr.” 276c.]] — __I.2 by inversion, preceding the fact explained, since, as, Ἀτρεΐδη, πολλοὶ γ. τεθνᾶσιν Ἀχαιοί.. τῷ σε χρὴ πόλεμον παῦσαι [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 7.328]]; χρόνου δὲ οὐ πολλοῦ διελθόντος (χρῆν γ. [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 19.159, 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Politica” 1333a2, +others]] — __II.9 γ. τοι for surely.., [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Helena” 93, “Supp.” 564, etc.; οὐ γ. τοι 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 21.172, etc.]]; compare τοιγάρτοι. — __B POSITION: γάρ properly stands after the first word in a clause, but in Pocts it frequently stands third or fourth, when the preceding words are closely connected, as ὁ μὲν γὰρ.. [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Choephori” 641, compare 753: also in Prose, τὸ κατ᾽ ἀξίαν γὰρ.. 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Ethica Nicomachea” 1163b11]]: sometimes for metrical reasons, where there is no such connexion, as third [ [(4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 222.729, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 219 (all Lyric poetry)), fourth (5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Aves” 1545)]]; in later Comedy texts fifth [ [(4th-3rd c.BC: Menander Comicus 462.2); sixth (4th c.BC: Antiphanes Comicus 26.22); seventh (4th-3rd c.BC: Menander Comicus “Ἐπιτρέποντες” 531, “Pk.” 170, 3rd c.BC: Athenio Comicus 1.5)]]; once sixth in [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus, καιρὸς καὶ πλοῦς ὅδ᾽ ἐπείγει γὰρ κατὰ πρύμναν “Ph.” 1451.]] — __B.2 inserted before the demonstrative -ί, as νυνγαρί for νυνὶ γά; compare νυνί. — __C QUANTITY: γάρ is sometimes long in [ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus for the sake of meter, θήσειν γὰρ ἔτ᾽ ἔμελλεν 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.39; φωνῆς γὰρ ἤκουσα “hymnus ad Cererem” 57]].—In Attic dialect always short: [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 366, “V.” 217, “Lys.” 20 are corrupt.]]
G1064: γαστήρ, ἡ, — genitive έρος, γαστρός: dative -έρι, γαστρί (the longer forms in Epic dialect, Lyric poetry, and once in Trag., [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Cyclops” 220)]]: dative plural γαστῆρσι [ [5th c.BC: Hippocrates Medicus “περὶ νούσων” 4.54, γαστράσι 2nd-3rd c.AD: Dio Cassius Historicus 54.22]]:—paunch, belly, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 13.372, etc.]]; γ. ἀσπίδος the hollow of a shield, [ [7th c.BC: Tyrtaeus Elegiacus 11.24]]; belly or wide part of a bottle, [ [5th c.BC: Cratinus Comicus 190.]] — __2 the belly, as craving food, κέλεται δέ ἑ γ. [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 6.133; βόσκειν ἣν γαστέρ᾽ 17.228]]; γαστέρι δ᾽ οὔ πως ἔστι νέκυν πενθῆσαι, i. e. by fasting, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 19.225; ἐν γαστρὸς ἀνάγκαις 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 726 (Lyric poetry)]]; to express gluttony, γαστέρες οἶον [ [8th-7th c.BC: Hesiodus Epicus “Theogonia” 26; γ. ἀργαί 6th c.BC: Epimenides Philosophus 1; ἐγκράτεια γαστρὸς καὶ ποτοῦ 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 1.2.8, compare “Oec.” 9.11]]; γαστρὸς ἐγκρατής master of his belly, [ [[prev. author] “Mem.” 1.2.1; opposed to γαστρὸς ἥττων, [prev. work] 1.5.1]]; γαστρὶ δουλεύειν, χαρίζεσθαι, to be the slave of his belly, [ [[prev. work] 1.6.8, 2.1.2]]; γ. δελεάζεσθαι[ [[prev. work] 2.1.4; τῇ γ. μετρεῖν τὴν εὐδαιμονίαν 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 18.296]]; τᾶς γαστρὸς φείδεσθαι, com. of one who has nothing to eat, [ [3rd c.BC: Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus 21.41.]] — __3 paunch stuffed with mincemeat, sausage, haggis, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 18.44, 118, 20.25, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Nubes” 409.]] — __II womb, ὅντινα γαστέρι μήτηρ.. φέροι [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 6.58]]; ἐκ γαττρός from the womb, from infancy, [ [6th c.BC: Theognis Elegiacus 305]]; ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα big with child, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 3.32; ὗν ἔχουσαν ἐν γ. “PFlor.” 130.3 (3rd c.AD)]]; ἐν γ. φέρουσα [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Leges” 792e]]; ἐν γ. λαβεῖν conceive, [ [4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Historia Animalium” 632a28, “Anthologia Graeca” 11.18 (1st c.AD: Nicarchus Epigrammaticus), LXX.Gen.30.41, +others]]; συλλαμβάνειν variant [ [LXX.Gen.25.21, cf. NT.Luke.1.31; ἐς γ. βάλλεσθαι 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 3.28]]; κατὰ γαστρὸς ἔχειν Vett.[ [Val. 193.33; φέρειν “Geoponica” 16.1.3; also γυνὴ ἑπτὰ ἤδη γαστέρας δυστοκοῦσα 2nd-3rd c.AD: Philostratus Sophista “Vita Apollonii” 3.39. (Perh.for γραστήρ, compare γράω.)]]
G1065: γε, — Doric dialect and Boeotian dialect γα, enclitic Particle, giving emphasis to the word or words which it follows. — __I with single words, at least, at any rate, but often only to be rendered by italics in writing, or emphasis in pronunciation: τὸ γὰρ.. σιδήρου γε κράτος ἐστίν such is the power of iron, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 9.393]]; εἴ που πτωχῶν γε θεοὶ.. εἰσίν if the poor have any gods to care for them,[ [17.475; μάλιστά γε 4.366]]; ὅ γ᾽ ἐνθάδε λεώς at any rate the people here, [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Coloneus” 42, etc.: with negatives, οὐ δύο γε]] not even two, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.303, 20.286]]; οὔκουν φθόγγος γε not the least sound, [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Iphigenia Aulidensis” 9.]] — __I.2 with Pronouns: with pronoun of 1st pers. [ [4th c.AD: Perses Epigrammaticus so closely joined, that the accent is changed, in ἔγωγε, ἔμοιγε (also ἔγωγα _Laconian dialect_, but ἐγώνγα, ἰώνγα _Boeotian dialect_): in 8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus frequently with _Article_ used as _pronoun_, see at {ὅ γε}: with _demonstrative_ Pronouns, κεῖνός γε, τοῦτό γε, etc.: in Comedy texts coalescing with -ί final, αὑτηγί 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 784]]; τουτογί, ταυταγί, etc., [ [[prev. author] “V.” 781, “Pax” 1057, etc. (but ἐνγεταυθί “Th.” 646): after possess. Pronouns, ἐμόν γε θυμόν 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 20.425, etc.: frequently after _relative_ Pronouns, ὅς γε, οἵ γε, etc., οἵ γέ σου καθύβρισαν 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 1364; ὅς γ᾽ ἐξέλυσας δασμόν [prev. author] “OT” 35, etc.]]; ὅσον γε χρῄζεις even as much as..,[ [[prev. work] 365; οἷόν γέ μοι φαίνεται 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 329a]]: rarely with interrogative Pronouns, τίνα γε.. εἶπας ;[ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Troades” 241]]; ποίου γε τούτου πλήν γ᾽ Ὀδυσσέως ἐρεῖς ; [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 441.]] — __I.3 after Conjunctions, to emphasize the modification or condition introduced by the subjoined clause, πρίν γε, before at least, sometimes repeated, οὐ μὲν.. ὀΐω πρίν γ᾽ ἀποπαύσεσθαι, πρίν γε.. αἵματος ἆσαι Ἀρῆα [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.288, compare 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 2.127]]; πρὶν ἄν γε or πρίν γ᾽ ἄν, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 961, “Ra.” 78, etc.; ὅτε γε 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 84e; ὁπότε γε 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Coloneus” 1699; ἐπεί γε 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.3.9; ἐπειδή γε 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 6.18; ὅπου γε 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 2.3.11]]; εἴ γε, ἐάν γε, if that is to say, if really, [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 6.18, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedrus” 252c]]; also simply to lay stress on the condition, κἄν γε μὴ λέγω and if I do not.., [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 317]]; εἴπερ γε if at any rate, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 7.16.γ, 143]], etc.; ὥστε γε (variant{ὥς γε}), with infinitive, so far at least as to.., [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedrus” 230b; ὥς γ᾽ ἐμοὶ χρῆσθαι κριτῇ 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Alcestis” 801]]; ὥς γε or ὥσπερ γε as at least, [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 570, “OT” 715, etc.]]:—γε may follow τε, when τε is closely attached to the preceding word, ὡς οἷόν τέ γε μάλιστα [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 4.5.2, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 412b; ἐάντε γε [prev. author] “Plt.” 293d; οἵ τέ γε [prev. author] “Grg.” 454e:—for its use in opposed or disjunctive clauses, see below 11.3.]] — __I.4 after other Particles, καὶ μὴν.. γε, οὐ μὴν.. γε, with words intervening, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Memorabilia” 1.4.12, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Alcestis” 518, etc.]]; after ἄν in apodosi, when preceded by οὐ or καί, [ [[prev. author] “Ph.” 1215, “Or.” 784]]; ἄταρ.. γε but yet, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 448]]; καίτοι γε, see at {καί το; ἀλλά γε} (without intervening words) is falsa lectio in [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Hp.Ma.” 287b (to be read ἀλλ᾽ ἄγε), “R.” 331b (ἀλλά γε ἕν codices, ἀλλὰ ἕν γε 5th c.AD: Stobaeus, Joannes)]]; ἀλλά γε δή uncertain in [ [[prev. author] “Phdr.” 262a; later, 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus 2.394c, 2nd-3rd c.AD: Aelianus “De Natura Animalium - Ar.Byzantine Epit.” 10.49 codices: but,]] — __I.5 when preceding other Particles, γε commonly refers to the preceding word, while the Particle retains its own force: but sometimes modifies the sense of the following Particle, γε μήν nevertheless, πάντως γε μήν [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 232, compare 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Electra” 754, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus, etc.]]; Epic dialect and Ionic dialect γε μέν [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.703, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 4.195, 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 7.152; γε μὲν δή 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 661, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Trachiniae” 484; γε μέντοι 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 164a, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 2.3.9, etc.: γε δή]] frequently strengthens an assertion, [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 42, 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 2.62, etc.; οἰόμεθά γε δή 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Euthydemus” 275a (compare also 11.1)]]; γέ τοι, implying that the assertion is the least that one can say, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Vespae” 934, “Pl.” 424, 1041, etc.; γέ τοι 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 447b; γέ τοι δή 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 1171, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedrus” 264b; γέ τοί που [prev. author] “Lg.” 888e; γε δήπου [prev. author] “Phd.” 94a, etc.]]; γέ που at all events, any how, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 896, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 607d, 478a, etc.]]; for γε οὖν, see at {γοῦν}. — __II exercising an influence over the whole clause: — __II.1 epexegetic, namely, that is, Διός γε διδόντος that is if God grant it, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 1.390]]; κλῦθι, Ποσείδαον.., εἰ ἐτεόν γε σός εἰμι if indeed I am really thine, [ [9.529: hence to limit, strengthen or amplify a general assertion, ἀνὴρ.. ὅστις πινυτός γε]] any man—at least any wise man, [ [1.229]]; frequently preceded by καί, usually with words intervening, ἦ μὴν κελεύσω κἀπιθωΰξω γε πρός ay and besides that.., [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 73]]; παρῆσάν τινες καὶ πολλοί γε some, ay and a great many, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 58d; καὶ γελοίως γε [prev. author] “R.” 531a]]; frequently with the last term in an enumeration, ταύτῃ ἄρα.. πρακτέον καὶ γυμναστέον καὶ ἐδεστέον γε καὶ ποτέον [ [[prev. author] “Cri.” 47b; ὄψεις τε καὶ ἀκοαὶ καὶ.. καὶ ἡδοναί γε δή [prev. author] “Tht.” 156b; repeated, συνήγαγόν μοι καί γε ἀργύριον καί γε χρυσίον LXX.Eccl.2.8]]; rarely without intervening words, καί γε ὁ θάνατος διὰ τὴν μοίρην ἔλαχεν [ [5th c.BC: Hippocrates Medicus “περὶ ἑπταμήνου” 9, compare 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 11.7 codices; καί γε.. ἐκχεῶ NT.Act.2.18: hence,]] — __II.2 in dialogue, in answers where something is added to the statement of the previous speaker, as ἔπεμψέ τίς σοι.. κρέα; Answ. καλῶς γε ποιῶν yes and quite right too, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 1049]]; κενὸν τόδ᾽ ἄγγος, ἢ στέγει τι; Answ. σά γ᾽ ἔνδυτα.. yes indeed, your clothes, [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Ion” 1412]]; οὕτω γὰρ ἂν μάλιστα δηχθείη πόσις. Answ. σὺ δ᾽ ἂν γένοιο γ᾽ ἀθλιωτάτη γυνή yes truly, and you.., [ [[prev. author] “Med.” 817, compare 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 680, etc.]]; πάνυ γε yes certainly, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Euthyphro” 8e, etc.]]; οὕτω γέ πως yes somehowso, [ [[prev. author] “Tht.” 165c]]; sometimes preceded by καί, καὶ οὐδέν γ᾽ ἄτοπον yes and no wonder, [ [[prev. work] 142b, compare d, 147e]]; sometimes ironically, εὖ γε κηδεύεις πόλιν [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Iphigenia Taurica” 1212.]] — __II.3 to heighten a contrast or opposition, — __II.3.a after conditional clauses, εἰ μὲν δὴ σύ γ᾽.., τῷ κε Ποσειδάων γε.. if you do so, then at all events Poseidon will.., [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 15.49]] {γέα}; ἐπεὶ πρὸς τοῦτο σιωπᾶν ἥδιόν σοι.. τόδε γε εἰπέ at any rate tell me this, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 5.5.20; εἰ μὴ τὸ ὅλον, μέρος γ᾽ ἐπιβάλλει 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 18.272:—sometimes in the protasis, εἰ γὰρ μὴ ἑκόντες γε.. ἀλλ᾽ ἀέκοντας.. 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 4.120.]] — __II.3.b in disjunctive sentences to emphasize an alternative, ἤτοι κεῖνόν γε.. δεῖ ἀπόλλυσθαι ἢ σέ.. [ [[prev. author] 1.11; ἤτοι κρίνομέν γε ἢ ἐνθυμούμεθα ὀρθῶς τὰ πράγματα 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 2.40; πατὴρ δ᾽ ἐμός.. ζώει ὅ γ᾽ ἢ τέθνηκε 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 2.131, compare 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 10.504]]: also in the second clause, εἰπέ μοι, ἠὲ ἑκὼν ὑποδάμνασαι ἤ σέ γε λαοὶ ἐχθαίρουσι [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 3.214, compare 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 7.10.θ, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 1098f]] — __II.4 in exclamations, etc., ὥς γε μή ποτ᾽ ὤφελον λαβεῖν uncertain in [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Iphigenia Aulidensis” 70, compare 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Coloneus” 977, “Ph.” 1003, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 93, 836, etc.]]; in oaths, οὔτοι μὰ τὴν Δήμητρά γ᾽ variant in [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 698; μὰ τὸν Ποσειδῶ γ᾽ οὐδέποτ᾽ [prev. author] “Ec.” 748; καὶ ναὶ μὰ Δία γε 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Apologia Socratis” 20; καὶ νὴ Δία γε 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 1350, 1st-2nd c.AD: Dio Chrysostomus Sophista 17.4, 2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Merc.Cond.” 28, 4th c.AD: Libanius Sophista “Orationes” 11.59, etc.: with words intervening, καὶ νὴ Δί᾽, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, ἕτεροί γε.. 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 13.16; νὴ Δία, ὦ Ἀθηναῖοι, ὥρα γε ὑμῖν 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Historia Graeca (Hellenica)” 7.1.37]]; merely in strong assertions, τίς ἂν φιλέοντι μάχοιτ; ἄφρων δὴ κεῖνός γέ.. [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 8.209, etc.]] — __II.5 implying concession, εἶμί γε well then I will go (in apodosi), [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hercules Furens” 861; δρᾶ γ᾽ εἴ τι δράσεις [prev. author] “IA” 817, compare “Andr.” 239.]] — __III γε frequently repeated in protasis and apodosis, as πρίν γε.., πρίν γε, see[ [above 1.3; εἰ μή γε.. τινὶ μείζονι, τῇ γε παρούσῃ ἀτιμίᾳ 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 31.29]]; even in the same clause, οὐδέν γ᾽ ἄλλο πλήν γε καρκίνους [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Vespae” 1507, compare 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.187, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Phoenissae” 554, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 335b, “Grg.” 502a.]] — __IV POSITION: γε normally follows the word which it limits; but is frequently placed immediately after the Article, as ὅ γε πόλεμος [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.66, etc.]]; or the preposition, κατά γε τὸν σὸν λόγον [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 3.1.15; ἔν γε ταῖς Θήβαις 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 1380; or δέ, νῦν δέ γε 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 144e]]; τὸ δέ γε[ [[prev. work] 164b; δοῖμεν δέ γέ που ἄν [prev. author] “R.” 607d, compare “Phd.” 94a, etc.]]; frequently in retorts, ἁμές ποκ᾽ ἦμες ἄλκιμοι νεανίαι. Answ. ἁμὲς δέ γ᾽ εἰμές [ [“Carmina Popularia” 18]]; οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅτι λέγεις. Answ. ἡ γραῦς δέ γε οἶδ᾽, ὡς ἐγῷμαι [ [4th-3rd c.BC: Menander Comicus “Ἐπιτρέποντες” 577, compare 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Septem contra Thebas” 1031, etc.]]

ἡ γ. ὀμώμοχ᾽ ἡ δὲ φρὴν ἀνώμοτος 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hippolytus” 612: with Preps., ἀπὸ γλώσσης]] by frankness of speech, [ [6th c.BC: Theognis Elegiacus 63; φθέγγεσθαι 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “O.” 6.13 (but ἀπὸ γ. ληίσσεται, opposed to χερσὶ βίῃ]], of fraud opposed to violence, [ [8th-7th c.BC: Hesiodus Epicus “Opera et Dies” 322)]]; also, by word of mouth, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.123, 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 7.10, 2nd c.AD: Arrianus Historicus “Anabasis” 2.14.1; τῷ νῷ θ᾽ ὁμοίως κἀπὸ τῆς γ. λέγω 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Coloneus” 936]]; τὰ γλώσσης ἄπο, i.e. our words, [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Bacchae” 1049]]; ἀπὸ γ. φράσω by heart, opposed to γράμμασιν, [ [5th c.BC: Cratinus Comicus 122]]; οὐκ ἀπὸ γλώσσης not from mere word of mouth, but after full argument, [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 813]]; μὴ διὰ γλώσσης without using the tongue, [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Supplices” 112; ἐν ὄμμασιν.. δεδορκὼς κοὐ κατὰ γλῶσσαν κλύων 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Trachiniae” 747:]] —phrases: πᾶσαν γλῶτταν βασάνιζε try every art of tongue, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Vespae” 547]]; πᾶσαν ἱέναι γλῶσσαν let loose one's whole tongue, speak withoutrestraint, [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Electra” 596; πολλὴν γ. ἐγχέας μάτην [prev. author] “fragment” 929]]; κακὰ γ. slander, [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 4.283: _plural_, ἐν κερτομίοις γλώσσαις]], i.e. with blasphemies, [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 962 (Lyric poetry), compare “Aj.” 199 (Lyric poetry): βοῦς, κ ῇς ἐπὶ γλώσσῃ, see at {βοῦς, κλείς}.]] — __3 of persons, one who is all tongue, speaker, of Pericles, μεγίστη γ. τῶν Ἑλληνίδων [ [5th c.BC: Cratinus Comicus 293, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Fragmenta” 629 (assuming variant).]] — __4 ἡ γ. τοῦ ταμιείου the advocacy of the fiscus, [ [2nd-3rd c.AD: Philostratus Sophista “Vitae Sophistarum” 2.29.]] — __II language, ἄλλη δ᾽ ἄλλων γ. μεμιγμένη [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 19.175, compare 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.804]]; γλῶσσαν ἱέναι speak a language or dialect, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.57]]; γ. Ἑλληνίδα, Δωρίδα ἱέναι, [ [[prev. author] 9.16, 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 3.112, compare 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Persae” 406, “Ch.” 564; γλῶσσαν νομίζειν 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.142, 4.183; γλώσσῃ χρῆσθαι [prev. author] 4.109; κατὰ τὴν ἀρχαίαν γ. 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Rhetorica” 1357b10]]; dialect, ἡ Ἀττικὴ γ. [ [4th c.BC: Demetrius Phalereus Rhetor “Demetrius on Style” 177; but also Δωρὶς διάλεκτος μία ὑφ᾽ ἥν εἰσι γ. πολλαί 3rd-4th c.AD: Tryphiodorus Epicus cited in Scholia 2nd c.BC: Dionysius Thrax Grammaticus p.320 H.]] — __II.2 obsolete or foreign word, which needs explanation, [ [4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Rhetorica” 1410b12, “Po.” 1457b4, 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus 2.406f: hence Γλῶσσαι, title of works by Philemon and others.]] — __II.3 people speaking a distinct language,[ [LXX.Jdt.3.8 (_plural_), interpolated in 4th c.BC(?): Scylax Geographus 15.]] — __III anything shaped like the tongue [ [compare (γλῶσσαι ὡσεὶ πυρός NT.Act.2.3).]] — __III.1 in Music, rced or tongue of a pipe, [ [4th c.BC: Aeschines Orator 3.229, 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Historia Animalium” 565a24, 4th-3rd c.BC: Theophrastus Philosophus “Historia Plantarum” 4.11.4, etc.]] — __III.2 tongue or thong of leather, shoe-latchet, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Comicus 51, 4th c.BC: Aeschines Socraticus Philosophus 57.]] — __III.3 tongue of land, [ [2nd c.AD: Appianus Historicus “Αιβυκή” 121, compare 95.]] — __III.4 ingot, γ. χρυσῆ [ [LXX.Josh.7.21.]] — __III.5 marking on the liver, in divination, [ [5th c.AD(?): Hesychius Legal icographus (γλῶσσα]] from γλωχ-y[acaron], compare γλώξ, γλωχί; γλάσσα from *γλᾰχ-y[acaron], weak grade of same root.)

G1418: δῠσ-, — insepar. Prefix, opposed to εὖ, un-, mis-, with notion of hard, bad, unlucky, etc., as δυσήλιος, δύσαγνος; destroying the good sense of a word, or increasing its bad sense: hence, joined even to words expressing negation, as δυσάμμορος, δυσανάσχετο; poetry in strong contrasts, as Πάρις Δύσπαρις, γάμος δύσγαμος. Before στ, σθ, σπ, σφ, σχ, the final ς was omitted, see δυστ-. (Cf. Sanskrit du[snull]-, dur-, e.g. durmanās, ={δυσμενής}; ONorse tor-, e.g. torsóttligr (δύσμαχος); OIr. du-, do-, e.g. dochruth 'misshapen'.)

Ποσειδῶνος all the gods, and above all.. , [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Persae” 750, etc.; ἐχθροὶ κ. ἔχθιστοι 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 7.68; τινὲς κ. συχνοί 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 455c]]; frequently ἄλλοι τε καί.., ἄλλως τε καί.., see at {ἄλλος} [ [11.6, ἄλλως 1.3]]; ὀλίγου τινὸς ἄξια κ. οὐδενός little or nothing, [ [[prev. author] “Ap.” 23a: joined with the _demonstrative_ _pronoun_ οὗτος (which see), εἶναι.. δούλοισι, κ. τούτοισι ὡς δρηπέτῃσι 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 6.11, compare 1.147]]; κ. ταῦτα and this too.. , γελᾶν ἀναπείθειν, κ. ταῦθ᾽ οὕτω πολέμιον ὄντα τῷ γέλωτι [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 2.2.16, etc.]] — __A.II at the beginning of a sentence, — __A.II.1 in appeals or requests, καί μοι δὸς τὴν Χεῖρα [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 23.75]]; καί μοι λέγε.., καί μοι ἀπόκριναι.., [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Euthyphro” 3a, “Grg.” 462b]]; frequently in Oratt., καί μοι λέγε.. τὸ ψήφισμα, καί μοι ἀνάγνωθι.., [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 18.105, 5th c.BC: Lysias Orator 14.8, etc.]] — __A.II.2 in questions, to introduce an objection or express surprise, κ. τίς τόδ᾽ ἐξίκοιτ᾽ ἂν ἀγγέλων τάχο; [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 280]]; κ. πῶς..; pray how..? [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Phoenissae” 1348]]; κ. δὴ τί..; but then what..? [ [[prev. author] “Hel.” 101]]; κ. ποῖον..; [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 462]]; κ. τίς εἶδε πώποτε βοῦς κριβανίτα; [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 86]]; κἄπειτ᾽ ἔκανε; [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Medea” 1398 (_anapaest meter_)]]; κ. τίς πώποτε Χαριζόμενος ἑτέρῳ τοῦτο εἰργάσατ; [ [5th c.BC: Antipho Orator 5.57, compare 4th c.BC: Isaeus Orator 1.20, 5th-6th c.BC: Isocrates Orator 12.23, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Theaetetus” 163d, +others]] — __A.II.3 ={καίτοι}, and yet, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 1245, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hercules Furens” 509.]] — __A.II.4 at the beginning of a speech, [ [5th c.BC: Lysias Orator “Fragmenta” 36a.]] — __A.III after words implying sameness or like ness, as, γνώμῃσι ἐχρέωντο ὁμοίῃσι κ. σύ they had the same opinion as you, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 7.50, compare 84]]; ἴσον or ἴσα κ..., [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 611, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Electra” 994]]; ἐν ἴσῳ (i.e. ἐστὶ) κ. εἰ.. Θηβαίοις εὐθὺς ἐπεβούλευσαν [ [5th-6th c.BC: Isocrates Orator 8.98.]] — __A.IV joining an affirmative clause with a negative, ἀλλ᾽ ὥς τι δράσων εἷρπε κοὐ θανούμενος [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Trachiniae” 160, etc.]] — __A.V καί.., καί.. correlative, not only.., but also.. , κ. ἀεὶ κ. νῦν, κ. τότε κ. νῦν, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 523a, “Phlb.” 60b; κ. κατὰ γῆν κ. κατὰ θάλατταν 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.1.7.]] — __A.VI by anacoluthon, ὣς φαμένη κ. κερδοσύνῃ ἡγήσατ᾽ Ἀθήνη, for ὣς ἔφη κ..., [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 22.247]]; ἔρχεται δὲ αὐτή τε.. κ. τὸν υἱὸν ἔχουσα, for κ. ὁ υἱός, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Institutio Cyri (Cyropaedia)” 1.3.1; ἄλλας τε κατηγεόμενοί σφι ὁδούς, κ. τέλος ἐγίνοντο 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 9.104; τοιοῦτος ὤν, κᾆτ᾽ ἀνὴρ ἔδοξεν εἶναι 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 392, compare “Nu.” 624.]] — __B even, also, just, — __B.1 τάχα κεν κ. ἀναίτιον αἰτιόῳτο even the innocent, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 11.654, compare 4.161, etc.]]; δόμεναι κ. μεῖζον ἄεθλον an even greater prize, [ [23.551, compare 10.556, 5.362: with numerals, κ. πέντε]]full five,[ [23.833; γενομένης κ. δὶς ἐκκλησίας 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.44, compare 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 2.44, 60, 68, +others (but ἐτῶν δύο κ. τριῶν]] two or three, [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.82, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “de Equitandi ratione” 4.4).]] — __B.2 also, κ. ἐγώ I also, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 4.40]]; κ. αὐτοί they also, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 3.4.44, etc.]]; Ἀγίας καὶ Σωκράτης κ. τούτω ἀπεθανέτην likewise died, [ [[prev. work] 2.6.30]]; in adding surnames, etc., Ὦχος ὁ κ. G2974: κωφ-ός, ή, όν, — blunt, dull, obtuse, opposed to ὀξύς, κ. βέλος [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 11.390, compare 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Fragmenta” 495.27; κ. καλάμη “Anthologia Graeca” 12.25 (1st c.BC-1st c.AD: Statyllius Flaccus Epigrammaticus).]] — __II metaphorically, — __II.1 of sound, mute, noiseless, κύματι κωφῷ [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 14.16]]; κωφὴν γὰρ δὴ γαῖαν ἀεικίζει is maltreating dumb, senseless earth, [ [24.54]]; τὰ μὲν ἄλλα ἔσκε κωφά the other parts sounded dull, opposed to to the ringing of the hollow parts when struck, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 4.200]]: neuter plural as adverb, κωφὰ δὲ πόντος κεῖτο [ [5th-6th c.AD: Orphica “Argonautica” 1103]]; ὁ κ. λιμήν, probably the bay of Munychia, as opposed to to the noisy Piraeus, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Historia Graeca (Hellenica)” 2.4.31]]; κωφότερος ὁ ψόφος ἔσται, i.e. muffled, [ [4th c.BC: Aeneas Tacticus 19]]; τῶν μεταλλικῶν κωφότατος [ὁ σίδηρος] rings least, [ [1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus 2.721f; κωφοὶ ἄνεμοι 1st c.BC: Diodorus Siculus Historicus 3.51.]] — __II.2 after [ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus]], of men or animals, dumb, [ [4th-5th c.BC: Parmenides Poeta Philosophus 6.7, etc.]]; καὶ κωφοῦ συνίημι καὶ οὐ φωνεῦντος ἀκούω Oracle texts cited in [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.47]]; οὐ.. παρὰ κωφὸν ὁ τυφλὸς ἔοικε λαλῆσαι, i.e. is not so dumb but that he will answer the blind fool who assails him, [ [5th c.BC: Cratinus Comicus 6; κωφότερος κίχλης 4th c.BC: Eubulus Comicus 29]]; κ. χάρις a mute gift (i.e. an epitaph), [ [“epigram Gr.” 298 (from Teos)]]; so κωφοῖς δάκρυσι [ [“IPE” 2.299 (from Panticapaeum)]]; κ. τάφοι probably in [ [“IG” 12(8).441.26]]; κ. προσωπεῖον mute figure on the stage, [ [1st c.AD: Philo Judaeus 2.520, compare 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus 2.791e; κ. πρόσωπον 1st c.BC: Cicero, M. Tullius Orator et Philosophus “Epistulae ad Atticum” 13.19.3]]; κ. καὶ ἄλογος, of a house, with no echoes, [ [2nd c.AD: Lucianus Sophista “Dom.” 1.]] — __II.2.b deaf, [ [hymnus ad Mercurium 92, 1st c.AD(?): Heraclitus 34. 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Septem contra Thebas” 202, “Ch.” 881; λήθην κωφήν, ἄναυδον 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Fragmenta” 670]]; ὅσοι γίνονται κ. ἐκ γενετῆς, πάντες καὶ ἐνεοὶ γίνονται [ [4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Historia Animalium” 536b3]] (hence of a deaf and dumb person, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.34, “BGU” 1196.49 (1st c.BC),compare 5th c.AD(?): Hesychius Legal icographus); with _genitive_, κωφὴ ἀκοῆς αἴσθησις 4th c.BC: Antiphanes Comicus 196.5, conjecture in 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Leges” 932a]]; κ. Ἑλλάδος φωνᾶς deaf of one's Greek ear, i.e. ignorant of Greek, [ [“Dialexeis 5th c.BC” 6.12; σπαράγματα κωφὰ τοῦ βεβαιοῦντος 1st-2nd c.AD: Plutarchus Biographus et Philosophus 2.1108d.]] — __II.2.c metaphorically, νοῦς ὁρῇ καὶ νοῦς ἀκούει· τἆλλα κωφὰ καὶ τυφλά [ [5th c.BC: Epicharmus Comicus 249; κ. πέτρος 4th c.BC: Moschio Tragicus Trag. 7; μαψαῦραι 3rd c.BC: Callimachus Epicus “Fragmenta” 67; ἐρημία 1st c.BC: Diodorus Siculus Historicus 3.40]]: neuter plural as adverb, κωφὰ χλιαίνεσθαι feebly, [ [Anthologia Graeca 12.125 (1st c.BC: Meleager Epigrammaticus).]] — __II.3 ὄμμα κ. vacant, lack-lustre eye, [ [4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Physiognomonica” 807b23.]] — __II.4 of the senses in general, dull, [ [4th-3rd c.BC: Theophrastus Philosophus “de Sensu” 19 (_comparative_).]] — __II.5 of the mind, dull, obtuse, ἐγὼ ὁ πάντα κ. G3305: Included with: μέν, — Particle, used partly to express certainty on the part of the speaker or writer; partly, and more commonly, to point out that the word or clause with which it stands is correlative to another word or clause that is to follow, the latter word or clause being introduced by δέ. — __A — __A.I μέν used absolutely to express certainty, not followed by correlative δέ, indeed, of a truth, synonymous with μήν, as appears from the Epic dialect and Ionic dialect form ἦ μέν in protestations and oaths (where Attic dialect used ἦ μήν), καί μοι ὄμοσσον, ἦ μ. μοι πρόφρων ἔπεσιν καὶ χερσὶν ἀρήξειν [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.77, compare 14.275; [ [8th-7th c.BC: Hesiodus Epicus “Opera et Dies” 563; πὰρ μέσον ὀμφαλὸν εὐδένδροιο.. ματέρος 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 4.74; γῆ μήτηρ 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Septem contra Thebas” 16, etc.; ὦ γαῖα μῆτερ 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hippolytus” 601]]; ἡ Μήτηρ, ={Δημήτηρ}, τῇ Μητρὶ καὶ τῇ Κούρῃ ὁρτὴν ἄγουσι [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 8.65]]; also of Rhea, [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “P.” 3.78; ὦ Πὰν.., Ματρὸς μεγάλας ὀπαδέ [prev. author] “fragment” 95, compare 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Helena” 1355 (Lyric poetry); μ. ὀρεία 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Aves” 746 (Lyric poetry); Γαλλαὶ μητρὸς ὀρείης φιλόθυρσοι δρομάδες “Lyrica Adespota” 121; M. θεῶν “SIG” 1044.8 (Halic., 4th c.BC)]]; as title of Isis, [ [“PPetr.” 3p.2 (compare p.xi) (3rd c.BC).]] — __3 frequently of one's native land, μᾶτερ ἐμά, Θήβα [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “I.” 1.1, compare “P.” 8.98, 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Septem contra Thebas” 416, 5th-6th c.BC: Isocrates Orator 4.25]]; and so, like{μητρόπολις}, [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “O.” 9.20, compare 6.100; ἡ Σκῦρος ἀνδρῶν ἀλκίμων μ. 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 326.]] — __II poetry, the origin or source of events, μ. ἀέθλων, of Olympia, [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “O.” 8.1; πειθαρχία γὰρ τῆς εὐπραξίας μ. 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Septem contra Thebas” 225; ἡ γνώμη κακῶν μ. 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 1361]]; of night, as the mother of day, [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 265]]; the grape of wine, [ [[prev. author] “Pers.” 614, compare 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Alcestis” 757; ματέρ᾽ οἰνάνθας ὀπώραν 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “N.” 5.6]]; Aphrodite of the Loves, [ [[prev. author] “fragment” 122.4]]; φάτις ὦ μᾶτερ αἰσχύνας ἐμᾶς, of a rumour, [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 174 (Lyric poetry)]]: also in Prose, γεωργίαν τῶν ἄλλων τεχνῶν μητέρα [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Oeconomicus” 5.17]]; πολιτειῶν μητέρες δύο (i.e. μοναρχία and δημοκρατία) [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Leges” 693d]]. (Cf. Latin mater, O[ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus]] módor, etc.)
G3385: Included with: μήτῐς — or μή τις, ὁ, ἡ, neuter μήτῐ, genitive μήτῐνος: (τὶς) old Gr. and Cretan dialect for μηδείς, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 12.272, +others, “Schwyzer” 175 (from Gortyn), “Leg.Gort.” 5.13, +others]]; Cretan dialect dative singular μηδιμί [ [“IG” 22.1130.4:]] —hence — __1 μήτι or μή τι, adverb, with imperative, and infinitive used imperatively, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.550, 5.130, etc.]]: with optative to express a wish, ὄλοιντο μή τι πάντες [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Trachiniae” 383.]] — __2 after Verbs of fear or doubt, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 11.470, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 2.67, etc.]] — __3 in direct questions, μή τί σοι δοκῶ ταρβεῖ; do I.. ? (i.e. I do not), [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 959, compare 249, LXX.Gen.20.9, NT.Mark.4.21.]] — __4 μή τί γε let alone, much less, οὐδὲ στρατιώτης οὗτός γε οὐδενός ἐστιν ἄξιος, μή τί γε τῶν ἄλλων ἡγεμών [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 21.148, compare 19.137]]; later, not to mention, οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ἀγγέλους κρινοῦμε; μήτι γε βιωτικά [ [NT.1Cor.6.3]]: with a word between, ὡς.. δώσοντι δίκην, μή τι ποιήσαντί γε [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 8.27; also μή τι δή 2nd c.BC: Polybius Historicus 12.8.6; μή τί γε δή, οὐκ ἔνι οὐδὲ τοῖς φίλοις.., μή τί γε δὴ τοῖς θεοῖς 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 2.23; also μητιγοῦν 2nd-3rd c.AD: Aelianus “Varia Historia” 12.9; μή τι δή γε 1st c.BC: Philodemus Gadarensis Epigrammaticus “Rh.” 1.261 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus, +others]]

G3703: ὀπώρ-α, — Ionic dialect ὀπώρ-η, ἡ: sometimes ὁπώρα, compare χεῖμα χὠπώραν, i.e. καὶ ὁπ-, [ [7th c.BC: Alcman Lyricus 76 (χειμάχωι πάραν, etc. codices)]]; proper nouns Ὁπωρίς [ [“IG” 5(1).1497, “Hopora” “CIL” 6.21782]]; compare μεθόπωρον, μεθοπωρινός:—the part of the year between the rising of Sirius and of Arcturus (i.e. the last days of July, all Aug., and part of Sept.), the latter part of summer; [ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus names θέρος and ὀπώρη]] together, θέρος τεθαλυῖά τ᾽ ὀπώρη [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 11.192]]; Σείριος being the star of ὀπώρη, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 22.27]]; compare ὀπωρινός.—In later times it became the name of a definite season, autumn (see. ὥρα [ [1.1 c)]], but was still used sometimes to denote summer (autumn being distinguished as φθινόπωρον or μετόπωρον), ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ τοῦ ἠρινοῦ χρόνου πρὸ ὀπώρας [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Historia Graeca (Hellenica)” 3.2.10, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Aves” 709, 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Meteorologica” 348a1; ἐπ᾽ ὀκτὼ μῆνας Κυρηναίους ὀπώρη ἐπέχει 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 4.199; νέας δ᾽ ὀπώρας ἡνίκ᾽ ἂν ξανθῇ στάχυς 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Fragmenta - American Journal of Philology” 304.7.]] — __II fruit, γλαυκῆς ὀπώρας.. ποτοῦ χυθέντος.. [prev. author] “fragment” 255.8; σικυούς, βότρυς, ὀπώραν 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Fragmenta” 569.1: so in Prose, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Historia Graeca (Hellenica)” 2.4.25, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Leges” 844d, 845c, 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “Historia Animalium” 606b2, 629a2]]: in this sense also in plural, [ [4th c.BC: Isaeus Orator 11.43; 7th c.BC: Alcman Lyricus (75)]] even calls honey κηρίνα ὀπώρ; ἐαρινὴ ὀπώρα [ [4th c.AD: Alciphro Epistolographus “fragment” 6.10.]] — __III metaphorically, life's summer, the time of youthful ripeness, [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “I.” 2.5]]; τέρειναν ματέρ᾽ οἰνάνθας ὀπώραν (see. οἰνάνθη) [ [[prev. author] “N.” 5.6]]; ripe virginity, [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Supplices” 998, 1015; ὀ. ὀσμὴν ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ (i.e. τοῦ νεκροῦ).. πεφευγότες [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 412; κακὴ ὀσμή [prev. author] “Ph.” 891: _plural_, βυρσῶν ὀσμὰς δεινάς 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Pax” 753; οἴνου ὀ. 2nd c.AD: Alexander Rhetor 222.4, 4th-3rd c.BC: Philemo Comicus 98.4]]: hence, scent, perfume, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Hiero” 1.4, 3rd c.AD(?): Achilles Tatius Astronomus 2.38]]; on ὀ. as affecting the sense,[ [compare 4th c.BC: Aristoteles Philosophus “de Sensu” 440b28f, “de An.” 421a7f, 4th-3rd c.BC: Theophrastus Philosophus “de Causis Plantarum” 6.1.1f]] — __II the sense of smell, ={ὄσφρησις}, [ [3rd c.AD: Democritus Epigrammaticus 11, 5th c.AD(?): Hesychius Legal icographus]] —The older form ὀδμή (compare ὄδωδα, ὄζ-ω, od-or) is alone used by [ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus, 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus, and 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus]]; G3778: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο, — genitive τούτου, ταύτης, τούτου, etc.: the dual feminine never in Attic dialect, see ὁ, ἡ, τό, [near the start]:—demonstrative pronoun, this, common from [ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus downwards]] — __A ORIGIN and FORMS: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο probably arose from a reduplication of the demonstrative ὁ, ἡ, τό with insertion of -υ- (= Sanskrit Particle u), e.g. ταῦτα from τα-υ-τα: Doric dialect genitive singular feminine τούτας [ [5th-6th c.BC: Philolaus Philosophus 11; _nominative_ _plural_ τοῦτοι, ταῦται 2nd c.AD: Apollonius Dyscolus Grammaticus “de Syntaxi;” 111.23: the former occurs 5th c.BC: Sophron Comicus 24, “GDI” 3045 B 6 (from Selinus), “SIG” 339.16 (Rhodes, 3rd c.BC)]], etc., the latter is uncertain in [ [5th c.BC: Sophron Comicus 97, certain in “SIG” 241 B 117 (Delph., 4th c.BC): in _Boeotian dialect_ all forms begin with οὑτ-]], as genitive singular neuter οὕτω [ [“Supp.epigram” 3.359.11 (3rd c.BC)]]; accusative singular feminine οὕταν [ [6th c.BC: Corinna Lyrica “Supp.” 2.80; _accusative_ _plural_ _neuter_ οὗτα “SIG” 1185.20 (Tanagra, 3rd c.BC), etc.: _genitive_ _plural_ _feminine_ _Attic dialect_ τούτων, Cretan dialect ταυτᾶν “Leg.Gort.” 5.19; _neuter_ ταύτων “Michel” 1334.10 (Elis, 4th c.BC).—In _Ionic dialect_ sometimes written ταότην, ταο̄τα, “SIG” 283.19 (Chios, 4th c.BC), 46.7 (Halic., 5th c.BC), +others]] —In _Attic dialect_ οὗτος was frequently strengthened by the _demonstrative_ -ί, οὑτοσί, αὑτηί, τουτί, _genitive_ τουτουί, _dative_ τουτῳί, _accusative_ τουτονί; plural nominative οὑτοιί, neuter ταυτί, etc., this man here: sometimes a Particle is inserted between the pronoun and -ί, as αὑτηγί for αὑτηί γε, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 784]]; τουτογί for τουτί γε, [ [[prev. author] “V.” 781, “Av.” 894, +others]]; ταυταγί for ταυτί γε, [ [[prev. author] “Eq.” 492, “Pax” 1057, +others]]; τουτοδί for τουτὶ δέ, [ [[prev. author] “Pl.” 227]]; τουτουμενί for τουτουὶ μέν, [ [[prev. author] “Ra.” 965.]] —In codices the ν ἐφελκυστικόν is sometimes added in the forms οὑτοσίν, οὑτωσίν, and οὑτοσίν is said to be Attic dialect by [ [2nd c.AD: Apollonius Dyscolus Grammaticus “de Pronominibus;” 59.24, 82.11]]. [This ι is always long, and a long vowel or diphthong before it becomes short, as αὑτη?~Xί, τουτω?~Xί, οὑτοῐί, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Nubes” 201, “Pl.” 44, “Ach.” 40, etc.]]] — __B USAGE in regard to CONCOR[ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator οὗτος]] is frequently used as a pronoun substantive: hence neuter is followed by genitive, κατὰ τοῦτο τῆς ἀκροπόλιος [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.84; εἰς τοῦθ᾽ ὕβρεως ἐλήλυθεν 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 4.37; εἰς τοῦθ᾽ ἥκεις μανίας [prev. author] 36.48; ταῦτα τῶν μαθημάτων 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Euthydemus” 278b: but quite as frequently as]] adjective, in which case its substantive commonly takes the Article, οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ or ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος.—But the Article is absent, — __B.1 always in Epic dialect Poets (except [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 18.114), οὗτος ἀνήρ 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 14.471, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 1.406, etc.]]: sometimes also in Trag., [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Persae” 122 (Lyric poetry), 495, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 406, “OC” 471, 1177: once in an Inscription, τοπεῖα: τούτων τὰ ἡμίσεα τοπείων “IG” 22.1622.135 (4th c.BC).]] — __B.2 sometimes when the Noun is so specified that the Article is not needed, ἐς γῆν ταύτην.., ἥντινα νῦν Σκύθαι νέμονται [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 4.8; ταύτας ἃς οἱ πατέρες παρέδοσαν μελέτας 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.85, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 449d, etc.; πατὴρ σὸς οὗτος, ὃν θρηνεῖς ἀεί 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Electra” 530.]] — __B.3 when οὗτος is used in local sense, here, see below with [ [1.5.]] — __B.4 when the Noun with which οὗτος agrees stands as its Predicate, αὕτη γὰρ ἦν σοι πρόφασις [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 1034]]; δικαστοῦ αὕτη ἀρετή [ἐστι] [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Apologia” 18a: this exception extends to cases in which the Predicate is not so distinctly separated from the Subject, αἰτίαι μὲν αὗται προυγεγένηντο]] these were the grievances which already existed, [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.66]]; ταύτην φήμην παρέδοσαν this was the report which.., [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Philebus” 16c: frequently with a _superlative_, κίνησις αὕτη μεγίστη δὴ.. ἐγένετο]] this was notably the greatest movement which.., [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.1, compare 3.113: with πρῶτος [prev. author] 1.55, 98, 6.31, NT.Luke.2.2.]] — __B.5 when 3rd pers. is used for 2nd pers. to express contempt, οὗτος ἀνήρ, οὑτοσὶ ἀνήρ, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 467b, 489b, etc.]] — __B.II though οὗτος usually agrees with the Noun that serves as Predicate, it is not rare to find it in the neuter, μανία δὲ καὶ τοῦτ᾽ ἐστί [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Bacchae” 305; τοῦτο γάρ εἰσι.. εὔθυναι 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 19.82, etc.]]: and in plural, οὐκ ἔστι ταῦτα ἀρχή [ [4th c.BC: Aeschines Orator 3.13; ταῦτ᾽ ἐστὶν ὁ προδότης [prev. author] 2.166]]: so with an explanatory clause added, τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν ὁ συκοφάντης, αἰτιᾶσθαι μὲν πάντα ἐξελέγξαι δὲ μηδέν [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 57.34.]] — __B.II.2 so also with a Noun in apposition, τούτοισιν μὲν ταῦτα μέλει, κίθαρις καὶ ἀοιδή [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 1.159; [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 4.23, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.5.10, etc.]] — __B.II.4 the neuter is also used of classes of persons, μελιτοπῶλαι καὶ τυροπῶλαι: τοῦτο δ᾽ εἰς ἕν ἐστι συγκεκυφός [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 854, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Leges” 711a]]; or of an abstract fact, οὐκ Ἰοφῶν ζ;—τοῦτο γάρ τοι καὶ μόνον ἔτ᾽ ἐστὶ λοιπὸν ἀγαθόν [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Ranae” 73.]] — __B.III with Prons., — __B.III.1 personal, οὗτος σύ, in local sense, see below — __B.III.2 interrogative, τί τοῦτ᾽ ἔλεξα; what is this that.. ? [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Philoctetes” 1173 (Lyric poetry), compare “Ant.” 7]]; ποίοισι τούτοι; for ποῖά ἐστι ταῦτα οἷς [ἔχεις ἐλπίδα]; [ [[prev. author] “OC” 388, compare “Ant.” 1049]]; Νέστορ᾽ ἔρειο ὅν τινα τοῦτον ἄγει whom he brings here, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 11.612.]] — __B.III.3 with οἷος, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 20.377, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 61c.]] — __B.III.4 possessive, πατὴρ σὸς οὗτος this father of thine, [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Electra” 530, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 7.3.30.]] — __B.III.5 demonstrative, οὗτος ἐκεῖνος, τὸν σὺ ζητέεις, where ἐκεῖνος is the Predicate, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.32; [στρατείαν] ἑνδέκατον μῆνα τουτονὶ ποιεῖται for these eleven months, [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 8.2, compare 3.4; τριακοστὴν ταύτην ἡμέραν 4th-3rd c.BC: Menander Comicus “Ἐπιτρέποντες” 27; ταύτας τριάκοντα μνᾶς 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 27.23, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 463b, etc.]] — __C SIGNIFICATION AND SPECIAL IDIOMS: — __C.I this, to designate the nearer, opposed to ἐκεῖνος, that, the more remote, ταῦτα, like τὰ ἐνταῦθα, things round and about us, earthly things, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 75e (variant)]]; compare ὅδε [near the start]: but οὗτος sometimes indicates that which is not really nearest, but most important, δεῖ.. τὸ βέλτιστον ἀεί, μὴ τὸ ῥᾷστον λέγειν: ἐπὶ ἐκεῖνο μὲν γὰρ ἡ φύσις αὐτὴ βαδιεῖται, ἐπὶ τοῦτο δὲ κτλ. [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 8.72, compare 51.3 and 18.]] — __C.I.2 when, of two things, one precedes and the other follows, ὅδε properly refers to what follows, οὗτος to what precedes, οὐκ ἔστι σοι ταῦτ᾽, ἀλλά σοι τάδ᾽ ἔστι [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Coloneus” 787, compare ὅδε III. 2: frequently, however, where there are not two things, οὗτος]] refers to what follows, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 13.377, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 2.306, etc.]]; οὔκουν.. τοῦτο γιγνώσκεις, ὅτι..; [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Prometheus Vinctus” 379, etc.]] — __C.I.3 οὗτος is used emphatic, generally in contempt, while ἐκεῖνος denotes praise, ὁ πάντ᾽ ἄναλκις οὗτος, i.e. Aegisthus, [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Electra” 301; τούτους τοὺς συκοφάντας 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Crito” 45a; so 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator “de Coron.” uses οὗτος of Aeschines, ἐκεῖνος]] of Philip; but οὗτος is used of Philip, [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 2.15, 4.3.]] — __C.I.3.b of what is familiar, τούτους τοὺς πολυτελεῖς χιτῶνας, of the Persians, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 1.5.8; οἱ τὰς κόρας ταύτας ὠνούμενοι τοῖς παισίν 1st-2nd c.AD: Dio Chrysostomus Sophista 31.153.]] — __C.I.4 in Attic dialect law-language, οὗτος is commonly applied to the opponent, whether plaintiff (as in [ [4th c.BC: Aeschines Orator 2.130)]] or defendant (as in [ [[prev. author] 1.1)]]; so, in the political speeches of [ [4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator, οὗτοι]] are the opposite party, [ [4.1, 8.7]], etc.; but in the forensic speeches, οὗτοι frequently means the judges, the court, [ [21.134, 36.47.]] — __C.I.5 much like an adverb, in local sense (compare ὅδε [near the start]), τίς δ᾽ οὗτος κατὰ νῆας.. ἔρχεα; who art thou here that comest.. ? [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 10.82]]; frequently in Attic dialect, τίς οὑτοσ; who's this here? [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 1048]]; πολλὰ ὁρῶ ταῦτα πρόβατα I see many sheep here, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Anabasis” 3.5.9 (as variant): with _pronoun_ of 2 _person_, οὗτος σύ]] ho you! you there! [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 532, 1121, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hecuba” 1280, etc.: and then οὗτος alone like a _vocative_, οὗτος, τί ποιεῖ; 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Supplices” 911,compare 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 71, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Alcestis” 773, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Equites” 240, “Nu.” 220, +others]]: with a proper name, ὦ οὗτος, Αἴας [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Ajax” 89; ὦ οὗτος οὗτος, Οἰδίπους [prev. author] “OC” 1627, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Vespae” 1364: with _vocative_, βέντισθ᾽ οὗτος 3rd c.BC: Theocritus Poeta Bucolicus 5.76:—the _feminine_ is rarer, αὕτη 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Medea” 922; αὕτη σύ 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Thesmophoriazusae” 610.]] —This phrase mostly implies anger, impatience, or scorn. — __C.II simply as antecedent to ὅς, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 2.40, 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Oedipus Tyrannus” 1180, etc.: frequently following _relative_ clause, ἅ γ᾽ ἔλαβες,.. μεθεῖναι ταῦτα [prev. author] “Ph.” 1247, compare 1319, “Ant.” 183, 203, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Gorgias” 469c.]] — __C.III = τοιοῦτος, οὗτος ἐγὼ ταχυτᾶτι [ [5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “O.” 4.26; σὺ τοίνυν οὗτος εὑρέθης 4th c.BC: Demosthenes Orator 18.282, compare 173.]] — __C.IV after a parenthesis, the Subject, though already named, is frequently emphatic repeated by οὗτος, οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ Ἀριστέης.., οὐδὲ οὗτος προσωτέρω.. ἔφησε ἀπικέσθαι [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 4.16, compare 81 (assuming variant), 1.146, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 107d, etc.]] — __C.V καὶ οὗτος is added to heighten the force of a previous word, ξυνεστῶτες.. ναυτικῷ ἀγῶνι, καὶ τούτῳ πρὸς Ἀθηναίους [ [5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 4.55, compare 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 1.147, 6.11, etc.; so οὐδὲ τούτου 4th c.BC: Aeschines Orator 2.100]]; see infr. VIII.2. — __C.VI repeated, where for the second we should merely say he or it, τοῖσιν τούτου τοῦτον μέλεσιν.. κελαδοῦντες [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Ranae” 1526, compare 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Laches” 200d.]] — __C.VII ταῦτα is used in some special phrases, — __C.VII.1 ταῦτ᾽, ὦ δέσποτα yes Sir (i. e. ἔστι ταῦτα, ταῦτα δράσω, etc.), [ [5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Vespae” 142, “Pax” 275, compare “Eq.” III; so ταῦτα δή [prev. author] “Ach.” 815; ταῦτά νυν [prev. author] “V.” 1008]]; so also ἦν ταῦτα even so, true, [ [5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Phoenissae” 417.]] — __C.VII.2 ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ὑπάρξει so it shall be, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedo” 78a.]] — __C.VII.3 καὶ ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ταῦτα so much for that, frequently in Attic dialect, as [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Symposium” 220c.]] — __C.VII.4 ταῦτα at end of a formula in epitaphs, etc., probably short for ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει or ὁ βίος ταῦτά ἐστιν, e.g. οὐδὶς (= -εὶς) ἀθάνατος: ταῦτα [ [“IG” 14.420; Προκόπι ταῦτα [prev. work]1824; χαίρεται (= -τε) ταῦτα [prev. work]1479, etc.: similarly perhaps in a letter, ἂμ μὴ πέμψῃς, οὐ μὴ φάγω, οὐ μὴ πείνω. ταῦτα “POxy.” 119.15 (2nd-3rd c.AD).]] — __C.VIII Adverbial usages: — __C.VIII.1 ταῦταabsolutely, therefore, that is why.., [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 11.694; ταῦτ᾽ ἄρα 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Acharnenses” 90, “Nu.” 319, 335, 394, +others, 5th-6th c.BC: Xenophon Historicus “Symposium” 4.55; ταῦτα δή 4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Persae” 159, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Symposium” 174a; ταῦτ᾽ οὖν 5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Trachiniae” 550, 5th-6th c.BC: Aristophanes Comicus “Vespae” 1358, etc.]]; αὐτὰ ταῦτα ἥκω, ἵνα..
