G5598: Ω, ὦ, τό, — twenty-fourth and last letter of the Ionic alphabet, ἀπὸ ἄλφα ἕως.ω. [ [“Corpus Glossariorum Latinorum” iii 283 (9th c.AD)]]; thence used as a symbol of the end, the last, ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ ἄλφα καὶ τὸ ὦ (not τὸ ὦ μέγα) [ [NT.Rev.1.8, +others]]:—as a numeral ώ = 800, but ωνυμ = 800, 000. The epichoric _Attic dialect_ and other alphabets of the Inscrr. had used o in differently to represent the sounds of the later ο and ω: Ω is a differentiated form of ο, and, though usually = ω, was used in the Ionic islands of Paros, Thasos, and Siphnos with the value ο, while O or O represented the sound ω. The name of the letter was τὸ ὦ (perispomenon accusative to [ [2nd c.AD(?): Helladius Epigrammaticus cited in Phot. p.530B.), compare 5th c.BC: Achaeus Tragicus 33.3, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Phaedrus” 244d, “Cra.” 420b, “Tht.” 203c]]: after the loss of the distinction between long and short vowels, ο and ω had the same pronunciation; they begin to be confused in Papyri of [ [3rd c.BC]](οἰκωνόμου [ [“PRev.Laws” 50.22 (3rd c.BC))]], but the name ω μέγα appears first in later Greek, [ [9th c.AD: Theognostus Grammaticus “Can.” 13; κατὰ σχῆμα διπλοῦ ω ¯ ἤτοι μεγάλου 12th c.AD: Eustathius Episcopus Thessalonicensis 869.26; οἱ δὲ περὶ Ἀρίσταρχον αὐτὸ τὸ ποτήριον ω ¯ μέγα εἶναί φασιν, ὁποῖν ἴσως τὸ κατὰ δύο ῡ ἐσχηματισμένον [prev. author] 869.29]]; ἐν τῷ ω ¯ μεγάλῳ under omega (in a lexicon), [ [[prev. author] 1828.49: διὰ τοῠ ω ¯ μεγάλου 2nd c.AD: Herodianus Grammaticus “Epim.” 208.]]

Diehl, 20 a. 11 (Epic style)]]; in Ionic dialect Prose, [ [5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 3.13, +others; rare in _Attic dialect_, and almost confined to certain phrases, see below 2, 3]]; ὥς simply ={οὕτως}, [ [4th-5th c.BC: Aeschylus Tragicus “Agamemnon” 930, 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 3.37, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Protagoras” 338a; ἀλλ᾽ ὣς γενέσθω 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Hecuba” 888, +others]] — __A.2 καὶ ὧς even so, nevertheless, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.116, +others]]; οὐδ᾽ ὧς not even so, [ [7.263, 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 1.6, +others, 5th c.BC: Herodotus Historicus 6.76; οὐδέ κεν ὧς 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 9.386: the phrases καὶ ὧς, οὐδ᾽ ὧς, μηδ᾽ ὧς,]] are used in Trag. and Attic dialect, [ [5th c.BC: Sophocles Tragicus “Antigone” 1042, 5th c.BC: Thucydides Historicus 1.74, 7.74; also later, “PCair.Zen.” 19.10 (3rd c.BC, unaccented), “UPZ” 146.40 (2nd c.BC), “GDI” 1832.11 (Delph., 2nd c.BC), “IG” 22.850.17 (3rd c.BC)]]; κἂν ὧς, εἴπερ μέλει σοι, ἀπόστειλόν μοί τινα [ [“POxy.” 120.11 (4th c.AD)]]; δουλεύων καθὼς καὶ ὧς [ [“GDI” 2160 (Delph., 2nd c.BC)]]; Thess. καὶ οὗς [ [“IG” 9(2).234.1 (3rd c.BC)]]; for this phrase the accentuation ὧς[ [is prescribed by Hdn.Gr.2.932, +others,compare 2nd c.AD: Apollonius Dyscolus Grammaticus “de Syntaxi”; 307.16, and is found in good Mss. of Homer; for the remaining uses under this head (Aa. 1, 3, 4) the accentuation ὥς is prescribed by the same grammarians.]] — __A.3 in Comparisons, ὥς.., ὡς.., so.. as.., etc.; and reversely ὡς.., ὣς.., as.. so, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 1.512, 14.265, etc.]]; in Attic dialect, [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 530d]]; also ὥς τε.. ὣς.., as.. thus.., [ [“hymnus ad Cererem” 174 - 6, 5th c.BC: Euripides Tragicus “Bacchae” 1066 - 8; οἷα.. ὥς [prev. author] “El.” 151 - 5]]; ὥσπερ.., ὣς δὲ.. (in apodosi) [ [5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Protagoras” 326d.]] — __A.4 thus, for instance, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 5.129, “hymnus ad Venerem” 218]]; ὥς should be accented in [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 5.121, 125.]] — __A.4.Ab ὡς, Relat., as, [ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus, etc.]]; properly relative to a demonstrative adverb, which is frequently omitted, κινήθη δ᾽ ἀγορὴ ὡς κύματα μακρὰ θαλάσσης, i. e. οὕτως, ὡς.., [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 2.144 (φὴ 4th-3rd c.BC: Zenodotus Grammaticus): it is _relative_ not only to the regular _demonstrative_ Advs. ὥς (ὧς), τώς, ὧδε, οὕτως, αὕτως, but also to ταύτῃ, 5th-6th c.BC: Plato Philosophus “Respublica” 365d, etc. We find a collateral _Doric dialect_ form ὥ (which see)]]; compare ὥτε. Usage: — __A.I in similes, frequently in [ [8th c.BC: Homerus Epicus, 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.161, +others]]; longer similes are commonly introduced by ὡς ὅτε, ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε, ἤριπε δ᾽, ὡς ὅτε πύργος [ἤριπε] [ [4.462: ἤριπε δ᾽, ὡς ὅτε τις δρῦς ἤριπε 13.389, compare 2.394]]; so later, [ [5th c.BC: Empedocles Poeta Philosophus 84.1, etc.; ὡς ὅτε θαητὸν μέγαρον, πάξομεν 5th c.BC: Pindarus Lyricus “O.” 6.2: ὡς ὅτε]] is rare in short similes, [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 11.368: ὡς]] is followed by indicative present, [ [8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 9.4, 16.364: also by]]aorist, [ [3.33f, 4.275, 16.823, +others]]; also by subjunctive present or aorist, [ [5.161, 10.183, 485, 13.334]] (sometimes ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἄν, [ [11.269, 17.520)]]; compare ὥστε A:—the Verb is sometimes omitted with ὡς, but may be supplied from the context, ἐνδούπησε πεσοῦσ᾽, ὡς εἰναλίη κήξ (i.e. πίπτει) [ [8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 15.479, compare 6.20; θεὸς δ᾽ ὣς τίετο δήμῳ 8th c.BC: Ilias Homerus Epicus “Illiad” 5.78; οἱ δὲ φέβοντο.., βόες ὣς ἀγελαῖαι 8th c.BC: Odyssea Homerus Epicus “Odyssey” 22.299: where ὡς]] follows the noun to which it refers, it takes the accent; so in Comedy texts, Ἀριστόδημος ὥς [ [5th c.BC: Cratinus Comicus 151, compare 4th c.BC: Eubulus Comicus 75.6]]; see infr.
